title: PEEL / PEE paragraphs
examples: When should I use PEEL instead of just writing about the character?
Can I use PEEL for poetry or only for stories?
What makes a 'strong' point in my paragraph?

explain.say: Today we are learning to write strong paragraphs using the PEEL method.

draw.text: P: Point, E: Evidence, E: Explain, L: Link

explain.say: First, you must make a clear point that answers the question directly.

draw.text: Point: State your main argument clearly.

explain.say: Next, you need to select specific evidence from the text to support your point.

draw.text: Evidence: Quote or specific detail from text.

explain.say: Then, you must explain how the evidence proves your initial point in detail.

items: Show the link between the two.

draw.text: Explain: Analyze how the evidence works.

explain.say: After explaining, you should link your idea back to the question or theme.

items: How does this affect the whole text?

draw.text: Link: Connect back to the overall theme.

explain.say: In real life, you use PEEL when writing a review about a film.

faq.q: How long should each part of the PEEL paragraph be?
faq.a: There is no exact length, but the explanation part should be the longest. It is where you show your thinking.
asks: Do I spend equal time on all parts?
Should my explanation be longer than my point?

faq.q: What counts as 'evidence' if I don't want to quote directly?
faq.a: You can use paraphrasing, which means putting the idea into your own words. Always mention where the idea came from.
asks: Can I summarize instead of quoting?

faq.q: If my point is very general, can I still write a good paragraph?
faq.a: A strong point must be specific and debatable. It should make a clear argument that needs proof.
asks: What if I am unsure of my point?
Does my point need to be a fact?

faq.q: What is the difference between 'explain' and 'link'?
faq.a: Explain shows how the evidence proves your point. Link shows why that point matters to the whole text.
asks: Do I need to link to the next paragraph?

faq.q: Should I use PEEL for all my literary analysis?
faq.a: PEEL is a very useful structure for building strong body paragraphs. It helps keep your argument focused.
asks: Can I use this structure for speaking too?

facts: A point is the topic sentence of your paragraph.
Evidence must be specific details or quotes from the text.
Explanation requires you to analyze the effect of the evidence.
The link connects your specific paragraph back to the essay's main theme.

quiz.say: A student writes: 'The character felt sad because the rain fell.' Which part of PEEL is missing?
quiz.show: The analysis of why the rain made them sad.
quiz.why: The student has a point and evidence, but they have not explained the emotional impact of the rain.

wrong.1: This is too general; it is a statement, but not a focused argument.
wrong.2: The rain falling is a detail, but the feeling of sadness is the interpretation.
wrong.3: A link must refer to the overall theme, not just the immediate sentence.

quiz.say: You use a quote about a character's clothing. This is best for which part?
quiz.show: The direct proof from the text.
quiz.why: Evidence is the factual proof, and a quote is the most direct form of proof.

wrong.0: A point is an argument, not a piece of quoted text.
wrong.1: Explanation happens after you present the evidence.
wrong.2: A link connects this small detail to the big idea of the essay.

quiz.say: A paragraph ends by saying: 'This shows how the theme of loss runs through the entire novel.' Which step did the writer complete?
quiz.why: The link always broadens the focus, connecting the small point to the large theme.

wrong.0: This is not the initial argument; it is a concluding thought.
wrong.1: It is not a direct quote from the book.
wrong.2: Explanation focuses on how the evidence works, not where it fits.
